About this guide

This is the day-to-day "how do I use this" guide for the web dashboards described in this document — Log Search UI, its Insights page, the LinuxDB Dashboard (fleet overview, per-host reports, and IdM Health), and the background monitoring/alerting mechanisms that email you when something needs attention. It's written for anyone on the team who needs to use these tools or troubleshoot a problem while the person who usually maintains them is unavailable — you shouldn't need anything beyond a browser, and for a handful of checks, SSH access to the relevant server.

If something breaks and you're reading this because of it: jump straight to When something looks broken — every troubleshooting table in this guide gives concrete steps to try yourself first.

Keeping this guide current: every time one of these tools changes in a way that affects how the team uses it (new feature, new tab, new troubleshooting step, a bug that changed expected behaviour), add a row to the Version History table above — that's how the team can tell, at a glance, whether anything they rely on has changed since they last read this.

Quick reference

Tool What it's for Default URL Default port Login
Log Search UI Search centralized syslog/journald logs across the whole fleet https://<admin1>:8081/ 8081 Yes — see Logging in
Log Search — Insights Alert-volume trends, severity breakdown, noisy-pattern detection over the same log data https://<admin1>:8081/insights 8081 Same login as Log Search UI
LinuxDB Dashboard Fleet-wide inventory + per-host diagnostic drill-down (disk, processes, health, hardware, config drift, IdM health) https://<admin1>:8082/ 8082 Yes — see Logging in
Monitoring & alerting Background checks that email you the moment something needs attention, instead of waiting for someone to open a dashboard n/a — arrives by email n/a n/a
This guide (live copy) This same document, always up to date, viewable from any browser — no SSH or repo access needed https://<admin1>:8082/guide 8082 Same login as LinuxDB Dashboard

<admin1> is the control node's hostname/FQDN — check your browser bookmarks or history, or a teammate who has used these pages before, if you don't already know it. Both apps use a self-signed TLS certificate by default in the lab (browsers will warn "not secure" / "not private" — that's expected, click through) unless a proper corporate-signed certificate has since been installed.

Logging in

Both dashboards sit behind a login before showing any data:

  • Local mode (the lab default): a single shared username/password. This is a shared secret and deliberately isn't printed in this guide — check wherever your team keeps shared credentials (e.g. a password manager or vault). To confirm which mode a given dashboard is actually running in without needing that secret, an admin on the host itself can check the deployed config file (/opt/log_search_ui/config.py or /opt/linuxdb_dashboard/config.py) for the AUTH_MODE value — it's plain text, not a credential.
  • Kerberos/AD/IdM mode (enabled via dashboard_auth_mode: kerberos): log in with your own existing domain username and password — same credentials you use elsewhere on the domain, nothing new to remember. If your login is rejected in this mode, it usually means either your account isn't in the required group for dashboard access, or there's a KDC/Kerberos reachability problem on the dashboard host itself — see When something looks broken.

Checking who's logged in

Every request to either dashboard is recorded in that service's own journal, including the username that was presented at login:

journalctl -u log-search-ui -f      # Log Search UI + Insights
journalctl -u linuxdb-dashboard -f  # LinuxDB Dashboard + this guide

Each line shows the source IP, the username, the timestamp, the request path, and the HTTP status (200 = succeeded, 401 = rejected):

10.20.30.41 - jsmith [14/Sep/2026 09:12:03] "GET /insights HTTP/1.1" 200 4213

In Local mode (the lab default — see Logging in above), this only tells you which username string was typed in, not which real person that was — everyone shares the same single username/password pair, so the log can't tell team members apart. It's still useful for confirming that someone logged in, from where, and when, and for spotting a run of 401s from the same IP (repeated failed attempts).

In Kerberos/AD/IdM mode, the same log line reflects each person's own domain username, so it becomes a genuine per-person access record for that app. For the authoritative record of the underlying authentication itself (not just what this app chose to log), the domain controller/IdM server's own logs are the source of truth — ask whoever administers your realm.

Log Search UI

What it's for: searching the centralized log database fed by rsyslog + journald across the fleet, instead of SSHing into each box and grepping flat files one at a time.

Search page

A single form: message pattern, host, syslog tag, severity, and a since/until time window.

  • Contains mode — plain, case-insensitive substring search (fast, the default; good for "does this word appear anywhere").
  • Regex mode — POSIX case-insensitive regex, for anyone used to grep -E pattern searches (e.g. Failed password.*root to match either order isn't valid regex, but sshd.*Fail(ed|ure) is — same regex rules as grep -E).
  • Results are paginated (500/1000/2000/5000/"All" per page) — Previous and Next preserve whatever filters you already set, they don't reset the search.
  • Every result table row shows enough context (timestamp, host, tag, severity, message) to decide if it's what you're looking for without drilling in further.

Common tasks:

  • "Did anyone fail to SSH into <host> recently?" — Host = <host>, Message = Failed password, since = last 24h.
  • "Show me everything from sshd on the whole fleet in the last hour" — Tag = sshd, since = last 1h, leave Host blank.
  • "I only remember part of the message and it might have different wording each time" — switch to Regex mode and use .* for the parts you're unsure of.

Insights page

A heuristics dashboard over a selectable time window (1h/24h/7d/30d):

  • Headline counters — SSH auth failures, sudo commands run, total password failures, distinct source IPs behind failed SSH attempts.
  • Alert volume over time — a stacked, severity-coloured bar chart. A bar that's mostly blue/grey is routine Informational/Debug noise; a bar with a red/orange cap is where something more severe happened in that window — hover any segment for the exact count.
  • Severity breakdown — a donut chart + table; click a row to jump straight to those raw log lines on the Search page.
  • Top repeated / similar alerts — clusters the noisiest recurring log lines and flags each cluster Likely noise or Review / Genuine? — this is the fastest way to spot a real, recurring problem (e.g. a service repeatedly throwing a permission error) without reading thousands of individual log lines. Start here if you're not sure what to search for.
  • CSV exports — a management summary and a full ops-detail report, for sharing outside the dashboard (email, ticket attachment, etc.).
  • Suppressing a known-noisy pattern — if something you already know about keeps cluttering Top repeated alerts, click Dismiss right on that row (or Dismiss all to suppress every occurrence of that pattern for that service). This takes effect immediately — no config change, redeploy, or service restart needed. To review or reverse a suppression later, open the Suppressed patterns section further down the Insights page and use Un-suppress.

Log Search — troubleshooting

Symptom Steps to try
Page won't load at all Try the URL again after a minute (the service may be mid-restart). If you have SSH access to the collector host: check systemctl status log-search-ui; if it's stopped, sudo systemctl restart log-search-ui, then journalctl -u log-search-ui -n 100 --no-pager for the reason it stopped (commonly a bad TLS certificate or a Python traceback — the last few lines usually name the exact cause).
Login rejected Confirm you're using the right credential type (local shared password vs. your own domain login — see Logging in). For Kerberos mode specifically, run kinit <your-username> on the dashboard host to test whether the domain/KDC accepts your password independent of the dashboard — if kinit itself fails, the problem is on the domain side, not the dashboard.
Search runs but returns nothing, even for something you know happened Double-check your time window and filters aren't too narrow (wrong host spelling, or "since" set later than the event). If filters look right, check the log database itself: sudo systemctl status postgresql on the log collector host — if it's stopped, sudo systemctl restart postgresql and retry the search a minute later.
A 500 error / "Internal Server Error" appears Check journalctl -u log-search-ui -n 100 --no-pager for the Python traceback (systemd captures it directly) — the last few lines usually name the exact cause (e.g. database connection refused, disk full). sudo systemctl restart log-search-ui clears most transient cases.

LinuxDB Dashboard

What it's for: a read-only view of the whole fleet's inventory and per-host diagnostics — patch status, disk usage, running processes, service health, hardware facts, and config-file drift — without logging into every server by hand.

Fleet overview

One table, one page: hostname/FQDN/IP, OS version, patch status (DNF_STATUS), whether a reboot is required, Satellite membership, last boot time and uptime, failed-service count, NTP sync state, and SELinux enforcement mode.

  • Jump to a host by name — type a hostname into the search box above the table and press Enter (or click View reports) to go straight to that host's detail tabs, instead of scrolling the table to find and click its link. Start typing and known hostnames appear as suggestions; an unrecognised hostname shows a message telling you it isn't valid rather than silently failing.
  • Click any column heading to sort by it — click again to reverse the order. The column currently sorted shows a bold, coloured heading with an underline and a solid arrow icon, so you can always tell which sort is active at a glance; every other heading shows a faint double-arrow to indicate it's clickable too.
  • History selector — step back to a previous captured run instead of only ever seeing "latest live" data. Useful for before/after comparisons around a patch window.

Per-host drill-down

Click any hostname to open tabbed detail for that host, all sourced from the same timestamped collection run (the run's timestamp is shown and independently selectable per tab):

Tab What's in it
Overview Identity/baseline facts: OS/kernel, patch & reboot status, Satellite membership, uptime, failed-service count, NTP/chrony sync state, SELinux mode, CPU/memory/swap sizing, hypervisor info, IPA realm
Disk & Filesystem Every mounted filesystem (type/size/used/use%/mountpoint), a filesystem-utilisation warning check, and an fstab-vs-mounted validation pass — the fast way to spot a filesystem nearing capacity, or an fstab entry that silently didn't mount
Processes Full process table (host/user/PID/command) plus a summary: process/user counts and top-CPU / top-memory consumers — the first stop when a host is reported "slow"
Server Health Load average, memory/swap, CPU iowait, inode usage, failed systemd services, key service state (sshd/firewalld/chronyd/auditd/crond), OOM/kernel errors, D-state processes, network errors, logged-on users, failed SSH/sudo attempts, locked accounts, SSSD/IdM/KRB5/DNS reachability, and certificate-expiry tracking for every IPA/PKI cert on the host
System & Hardware Info BIOS/baseboard/chassis facts, CPU model/socket/core/thread counts, memory slot population, private and public IPs
Installed Packages Every RPM package installed on the host — name, version, release, architecture and install date. See also Package Search below to search across every host at once.
Config Files Tracked security/ops config files (sshd_config, sudoers, firewalld.conf, krb5.conf, sssd.conf, audit rules, PAM stacks, etc.), each flagged Unchanged or Missing against the last captured baseline, with a link to the actual captured content
IdM Health (only shown for IdM-related hosts that have data) Latest ipa-healthcheck results for that host — see IdM Health below

Data freshness

Fleet inventory and per-host reports normally refresh automatically four times a day (every 6 hours) via a scheduled job on the control node — you don't need to do anything to keep this current. If a page shows "No hostinfo.csv found" or "No data yet for this host":

  • Check disk space on the data mount: df -h /linuxdb on the control node — a full filesystem is the most common reason a scheduled collection silently fails to write its output.
  • Check when the data actually last updated: ls -la /linuxdb/hostinfo (and the equivalent path for the report you're looking at) shows the last-modified time of the most recent run.
  • If you have access to the control node as the automation service account, the scheduled job's own output is logged under ~/ansible/logs/cron_hostinfo.log and ~/ansible/logs/cron_dashboard.log — tail -50 either file to see whether the last scheduled run actually succeeded and when it last ran.

IdM Health

The IdM Health tab shows a point-in-time snapshot from the latest ipa-healthcheck run against that host, refreshed on the same schedule as everything else in LinuxDB. For the separate, always-on email alert that fires the moment a real IdM problem is found (rather than waiting for you to open this tab), see Monitoring & Alerting below.

Package Search

A Package Search tab in the header (shown on every page) lets you search installed packages across the whole fleet in one go, instead of opening each host's Installed Packages tab in turn. Type a package name — e.g. "firefox" — and it lists every host that currently has it installed, with the exact version, release and architecture on each; click any hostname in the results to jump straight to that host's own Installed Packages tab. Click a column heading to sort the results by it, same as the fleet overview table. Results reflect whatever was captured on each host's last refresh (see Data freshness) — a package installed since then won't show up until the next scheduled or manual refresh.

LinuxDB — troubleshooting

Symptom Steps to try
Page won't load at all Try again after a minute (the service may be mid-restart). If you have SSH access: check systemctl status linuxdb-dashboard; if it's stopped, sudo systemctl restart linuxdb-dashboard, then journalctl -u linuxdb-dashboard -n 100 --no-pager for the reason it stopped.
Login rejected Same checks as Log Search UI — see Logging in and the kinit test above for Kerberos mode.
A host is missing from the fleet table entirely Check /linuxdb/hostinfo for that host's row and its timestamp (see Data freshness); on the control node, cat ~/ansible/inventory confirms whether the host is actually listed in the automation inventory at all.
A tab shows "No data yet for this host" Normal for a brand-new host until the next scheduled cycle — see Data freshness for how to confirm the last run's timing.
Table won't sort / clicking a heading does nothing Confirm you're clicking directly on the column heading text/icon, not the row below it; try a hard refresh (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+R) in case an old cached page is loaded. If it still doesn't respond, open your browser's developer console (F12) and check for a JavaScript error — that points to a front-end bug rather than missing data.

Monitoring & Alerting

Beyond the two dashboards above, several small, independent background mechanisms email you directly the moment something needs attention, instead of waiting for someone to open a dashboard or for the next scheduled report. All of them deliver mail through the same local mail relay already configured on the collector host — nothing to log into, they just land in your inbox.

The common pattern: most of these are a check + watcher pair. The check half runs locally on every monitored host on a short systemd timer and, when it finds a problem, writes one fixed-wording line to syslog — it never sends mail itself and needs no mail relay of its own. The existing log-forwarding pipeline carries that line to the collector like any other log message. The watcher half runs only on the collector, polls the log database for those specific messages, and sends the actual alert email (batched, not one email per line). Two mechanisms below don't follow this pattern — log_alerter reacts to any log line at or above a severity threshold rather than a specific fixed message, and host_availability_watcher checks hosts directly over the network rather than waiting for them to log anything at all.

Mechanism What it watches How often What triggers an email
Service failure (service_failure_watcher) Any systemd unit failing, on any log-forwarding host Collector polls every 30s Any unit entering the failed state
Log alerter (log_alerter) Every log line landing in the log database Collector polls every 60s Any line at or above a configured severity threshold
Host availability (host_availability_watcher) Whether each host responds to ping and its SSH port Collector checks directly every 60s A host's state changes: reachable → unreachable, reachable → SSH-only-unreachable, or back to reachable
Disk space (disk_space_check + disk_space_watcher) Real filesystem disk-space and inode usage on every host Per-host check every 5 min; collector polls every 60s Usage crosses 85% (WARNING) or 95% (CRITICAL)
Chrony/NTP (chrony_check + chrony_watcher) NTP sync state, chronyd running, chrony leap status on every host Per-host check every 15 min; collector polls every 180s NTP not synchronized, chronyd not active, or leap status abnormal
IdM health (idm_healthcheck_watch + idm_healthcheck_watcher) ipa-healthcheck findings on IdM hosts Per-host check every 30 min; collector polls every 60s Any non-SUCCESS finding, or the check itself failing to run

What to do when you get one of these emails:

  • Service failure — SSH to the named host and check systemctl status <unit> / journalctl -u <unit> -n 100 --no-pager, or look at that host's Server Health tab in LinuxDB for its failed-service count.
  • Log alerter — the email includes the matching log lines; open Log Search UI and search for the same host/text for full context around that time.
  • Host availability — the named host isn't responding to ping or SSH at all. Try reaching it yourself (ping, SSH, or your hypervisor/console access) before assuming the network path from the collector itself is the problem.
  • Disk space — open that host's Disk & Filesystem tab in LinuxDB to see every mounted filesystem's current usage, or check directly with df -h / df -i over SSH.
  • Chrony/NTP — check that host's Server Health tab (NTP sync state is listed there) or run timedatectl / chronyc tracking directly over SSH.
  • IdM health — check the IdM Health tab for that host in LinuxDB, or run ipa-healthcheck --output-type=json directly on the affected host for the full finding detail.

A note on an older mechanism: you may occasionally see references to a per-host service-failure alert that installed itself directly onto every monitored unit. That approach has been retired in favour of service_failure_watcher above, which covers the same need centrally from the collector without needing anything installed on individual hosts — if you run across it, it's legacy and not the active mechanism.

If you expect an alert email and it never arrives:

  • On the collector, check the relevant watcher's timer is actually running: systemctl status <watcher-name>.timer (e.g. disk-space-watcher.timer, chrony-watcher.timer).
  • Check the collector's local mail queue: mailq — a backlog there points to a mail-relay delivery problem rather than the watcher itself.
  • Check the watcher's own log for errors reaching the log database: journalctl -u <watcher-name> -n 100 --no-pager.

Control node scripts (on-demand / manual runs)

The scheduled collection described in Data freshness keeps everything current automatically, four times a day. The scripts below exist for when you need something sooner — an immediate recheck of one host, a full manual refresh outside the normal schedule, redeploying a dashboard after a code change, or patching a host. They live on the control node in the automation service account's home directory and need SSH access to that account to run — most of the team won't need these day to day, but they're documented here so anyone covering can use one without having to reverse-engineer what it does first.

Fleet data refresh

Script What it does Notes
ansible_hostinfo.sh Refreshes hostinfo.csv — the fleet Overview table, and each host's Overview tab (OS/kernel, patch status, uptime, etc.). Interactive: asks which host or inventory group to refresh. Press Enter alone to refresh the whole fleet (the default).
ansible_linuxdb.sh The full manual refresh: refreshes hostinfo.csv for the whole fleet, re-collects every per-host diagnostic report (Disk & Filesystem, Processes, Server Health, System & Hardware Info), re-captures the tracked config files, and redeploys the LinuxDB Dashboard service itself. Not interactive — always targets the whole fleet. Briefly restarts the LinuxDB Dashboard service while it redeploys, so expect a few seconds of "page won't load" on that dashboard only.

One-off diagnostic checks (ad hoc — not saved to the dashboard)

These five push one of the same check scripts the scheduled collection normally runs out to a host (or group) of your choosing, and print its output straight to your screen there and then. They're useful for an immediate answer without waiting for the next scheduled run — but the result only ever appears in your terminal; it is not saved into the dashboard's history, so the matching tab won't reflect it.

Script Same check as tab What it looks at
ansible_df_check.sh Disk & Filesystem Per-mount filesystem usage (WARNING at 85%, CRITICAL at 95%), and whether currently mounted filesystems match /etc/fstab.
ansible_proc_check.sh Processes Every non-system-account process running on the host (user, PID, command).
ansible_svr_check.sh Server Health Load average, memory/swap, CPU/iowait, inode usage, failed systemd services, key service state, OOM/kernel errors, logged-in users, failed SSH/sudo attempts, IdM/DNS reachability, and certificate expiry.
ansible_system_stats.sh System & Hardware Info BIOS/baseboard/chassis facts, CPU topology, memory slot population, and network device/IP info.
ansible_rpm_report.sh Installed Packages Every installed package on the host, with its version, release, architecture and install date.

All five are interactive and always ask for a target host or inventory group by name — there's no default, so have the hostname (or group) ready before you start.

Additional ad hoc reports

A few more read-only reports that don't have a matching dashboard tab — each writes its result to a file on the control node (or straight to your screen) rather than into LinuxDB or Log Search.

Script What it reports Where the output goes
ansible_ilo_inventory.sh HPE firmware/BIOS/iLO version and storage-controller info for every physical host in the hpe_ilo_hosts group. CSV at /var/tmp/hpe_firmware_inventory.csv on the control node. Not interactive — always runs against the whole hpe_ilo_hosts group.
ansible_dnf_history.sh Each targeted host's most recent patch transaction — packages installed/upgraded/removed and when it ran. CSV at /tmp/dnf_history_report.csv on the control node. Interactive: asks for a target host/group (defaults to the whole fleet if you just press Enter).
ansible_critical_alerts.sh A 30-day scan per host for critical/kernel issues, failed services, authentication failures, disk/filesystem errors, and recent reboots. Per-host report plus one consolidated report under /var/tmp/server-findings/ on the control node. Interactive: asks for a target host/group (defaults to the whole fleet if you just press Enter).
ansible_idm_healthcheck.sh The same ipa-healthcheck findings behind the IdM Health tab, run on demand — useful right after patching or rebooting an IdM host rather than waiting for the next scheduled check. Printed to your screen only. Interactive: asks for a target host/group — type the actual IdM host/group rather than accepting the fleet-wide default, since this only makes sense against IdM servers.
ansible_sudo_audit.sh A fleet-wide audit of every sudoers/sudoers.d rule, flagging root-equivalent and NOPASSWD grants for review. CSV at /var/tmp/sudo_audit_report.csv on the control node, restricted to owner-read-only — it lists privileged access per host, so treat it accordingly. Not interactive — always fleet-wide.
ansible_system_health_report.sh Uptime, load average, network totals, and the status of key services (sshd, firewalld, multipathd) for every host in the fleet. Printed to your screen, plus a copy per host under playbooks/reports/ on the control node. Not interactive — always fleet-wide.
ansible_lineage.sh Traces a process, port, open file, or container on a chosen host back to the systemd unit, cron job, SSH session, or shell actually responsible for it. Printed to your screen only. Fully interactive — asks for the target host, then whichever of process/PID/port/file/container you want to check (press Enter to skip any that don't apply).

As with the checks above, none of these results are saved into the dashboards — each run only produces its file (or screen output) at the time you run it.

Redeploying the web dashboards after a code change

Only relevant if a dashboard's code has just been changed — these pull in the newest version and restart the affected service. Running one against unchanged code is harmless (it just restarts the service), but there's no reason to run them otherwise.

Script What it redeploys
ansible_pushdb_change.sh LinuxDB Dashboard only.
ansible_push_logsearch_change.sh Log Search UI (Search + Insights) only.
ansible_push_all_changes.sh Both of the above, one after the other — use this when a change touched both apps (e.g. a shared header/navigation update). Stops at the first failure rather than pushing the second app on top of a broken first one.

Each briefly restarts the corresponding service — expect a few seconds of "page won't load" on that dashboard while it happens.

Patching

Script What it does Notes
ansible_update_system.sh Patches a host or inventory group and reboots automatically afterwards if the patch requires it. Interactive: asks for the target host/group, then whether to auto-reboot (defaults to yes if you just press Enter). Hosts are patched in batches (30% of the target group at a time by default), not all at once, so a group patch doesn't take everything down together.

Time synchronization (chrony via Red Hat System Roles)

Playbook What it does Notes
ansible-playbook playbooks/deploy_timesync_role.yml (run from the control node) Deploys/updates the chrony (NTP) configuration on the target host(s) via Red Hat's redhat.rhel_system_roles.timesync role and restarts chronyd if it changed. Interactive: asks for the target host/group, with no default — you must type it explicitly. Idempotent and safe to re-run: chronyd is only restarted when the configuration actually changed, so expect a short gap in NTP sync only in that case.

This is the only supported way to (re)deploy chrony configuration — the repo's previous own-template deployment scripts were removed. What you need to know as an operator:

Question Answer
NTP servers The effective chrony_ntp_servers YAML list for each host: group_vars/all/site_hosts.yml supplies the default; group_vars/<realm_group>/site_hosts.yml can override it per realm. Do not use comma-separated INI values. The home lab overrides this in group_vars/homelab.yml: clients sync from idm1 (which serves NTP to the lab subnets — the playbook adds the allow directives), with the public pool as fallback; idm1 itself tracks the pool directly.
Does monitoring change? No. chrony_check / chrony_watcher alerting checks whatever chrony configuration is actually running.
Collection dependency redhat.rhel_system_roles — not on public Galaxy; it ships as the AppStream rhel-system-roles RPM (sudo dnf install rhel-system-roles on the control node).

Details, caveats, and the offline collection install steps live in rhel_system_roles/README.md.

Powering off hosts

Use these deliberately, not casually — both genuinely power hosts off. Two scripts exist; pick based on how strong a guarantee you need that a host is actually off, not just unreachable over the network:

Script Guarantee Use when
ansible_system_poweroff.sh Hardware-confirmed for hosts in the hpe_ilo_hosts group — checks the physical iLO/IPMI management interface directly, independent of the OS. Falls back to a network check for everything else. You have iLO/BMC access in place and need to be certain a physical host is actually powered down (e.g. before physically removing a drive).
ansible_poweroff_all.sh Network reachability only, for every host, physical or virtual — proves the host stopped answering on a port, not that the hardware itself is off. A same-day power-down where there's no time to validate the iLO/IPMI path, or the target group is entirely virtual.

Both scripts follow the same safe sequence:

  1. Ask for the target host or inventory group.
  2. Print the exact host list that would be affected, before touching anything.
  3. Require you to type YES in full capitals to continue — pressing Enter, or typing anything else, aborts with nothing powered off.
  4. Shut hosts down one at a time by default, in inventory order, so a clustered/replicated service never loses more than one member at once.

Review the printed host list carefully before typing YES — that is the only safety check standing between you and the hosts actually shutting down.

When something looks broken

A quick decision guide, in order:

  1. Can you reach the page at all? - No → the underlying service may be down or the host may be unreachable. If you have SSH access to the collector host, check systemctl status log-search-ui / linuxdb-dashboard and sudo systemctl restart <service>, then journalctl -u <service> -n 100 --no-pager for the reason it stopped.
  2. Page loads, but login fails? - Confirm you're using the right kind of credential (see Logging in). For Kerberos mode, run kinit <your-username> on the dashboard host to test the domain/KDC independently of the dashboard.
  3. Page loads and you're logged in, but the data looks wrong, missing, or stale? - Work through Data freshness: check disk space on /linuxdb, the last-modified time of the relevant data file, and the scheduled job's own log output.
  4. Got an alert email and want to investigate? - See Monitoring & Alerting above for what each alert type means and where to look next.
  5. Everything above looks fine, but something still seems off? - Note exactly which page, what you expected vs. what you actually saw, and roughly when you first noticed it, then check journalctl -u log-search-ui / linuxdb-dashboard -n 200 --no-pager around that time — most issues leave a trace there even when nothing else points to an obvious cause.
